title: When the Trip Goes Wrong
subtitle: Three short situations: the connection you missed, the bag that did not arrive, and the room that is not what you booked.
description: An A2 listening and reading page for the part of travel the guidebooks leave out — a missed connection, a lost bag and a wrong hotel room, and the small set of English phrases that gets each of them fixed.
source: authored for this site; no source document
passage: Nothing in travel teaches you English faster than something going wrong. Your lines are written out as models.
1. The connection you missed
You: Excuse me. My flight from Dallas landed late and I missed my connection to Denver.
Agent: Let me see your boarding pass. … Yes, the seven-forty has already left.
You: Is there another flight tonight?
Agent: There's one at ten-fifteen, but it's full. I can put you on the first flight tomorrow morning.
You: I'd rather not spend the night at the airport. Can you check whether another airline has something?
Agent: One moment. … There is a nine-thirty with a partner airline. Shall I rebook you on that?
You: Yes, please. And will my bag follow me automatically?
Agent: It should. Keep this tag in case it doesn't.
You: Thank you. Could I also have something in writing, for my insurance?
2. The bag that did not arrive
You: I waited at the belt for an hour and my suitcase never came.
Clerk: I'm sorry. Do you have the tag from check-in?
You: Here it is.
Clerk: Can you describe the bag?
You: It's a large gray suitcase with four wheels and a red ribbon on the handle.
Clerk: Thank you. It's still in Dallas. We'll put it on tonight's flight and deliver it to your hotel tomorrow.
You: I have nothing with me except hand luggage. Is there anything for that?
Clerk: You can claim up to a hundred dollars for the first night. Keep the receipts.
You: And how do I check where the bag is?
Clerk: With this file number, on our website.
3. The room that is not what you booked
You: Good evening. I have a reservation for three nights, under Palmer.
Clerk: Yes — a double room with a city view.
You: I booked a quiet room at the back. This one faces the main street.
Clerk: Let me look. … I'm afraid we're fully booked tonight.
You: I understand it isn't your fault, but I won't sleep with that noise. What can you do?
Clerk: I can move you tomorrow morning, and take twenty percent off tonight.
You: That works. Could you put the new room in writing, so I don't have to explain it again?
Clerk: Of course. And breakfast is on us.
You: Thank you. I appreciate it.

vocabulary.definition: to arrive too late to get on the next flight, train or bus
the ticket that lets you onto the plane
to put somebody on a different flight or date
a polite way of refusing: I would prefer not to
the moving band at an airport where suitcases come out
the small bag you carry onto the plane yourself
to officially ask a company to pay money back to you
the paper that proves you paid
a phrase that keeps a complaint friendly: the problem is not the person you are talking to

exercises.title: Getting It Fixed Politely
exercises.instructions: Choose the form that is both natural and polite.

items.prompt: The agent offers tomorrow morning. You do not want to sleep at the airport. You say:
options: I'd rather not spend the night here. Can you check another airline?
items.explanation: "I'd rather not" refuses softly, and the question gives the agent something to do. A flat "no" usually ends the conversation.

items.prompt: Complete: "My flight landed late and I ___ my connection."
items.explanation: In English you miss a flight, a train or a connection. "Lost" is a direct translation that English does not use here.
Fully booked = nothing left free. The same phrase works for restaurants and flights.

items.prompt: Why is "I understand it isn't your fault, but…" useful?
options: It keeps the clerk on your side while you still complain
It means you accept the room
items.explanation: It separates the problem from the person. The clerk can then help you instead of defending themselves.

items.prompt: You want proof of the new arrangement. You ask for it:
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is "in writing" — and asking for it is the single most useful habit when a trip goes wrong.

items.prompt: The clerk says "breakfast is on us." This means:
options: the hotel will pay for it
breakfast is already included in the law
items.explanation: "It's on us" / "it's on me" means the speaker pays.

items.prompt: I waited at the ___ for an hour and my suitcase never came.
items.explanation: The belt is the moving band the bags come out on.

items.prompt: Can you ___ me on the nine-thirty flight?
items.explanation: To rebook somebody is to move them to another flight.

items.prompt: I have a ___ for three nights, under Palmer.
items.explanation: The noun is a reservation (American English) or a booking (both are used).

items.prompt: Keep the ___ , because you can claim the money back.
items.explanation: A receipt proves you paid. A recipe tells you how to cook — a classic trap.

items.prompt: I only have ___ luggage, because my suitcase is still in Dallas.
items.explanation: Hand luggage is the bag you carry on yourself.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the conversations.

items.statement: The ten-fifteen flight has free seats.
items.explanation: False — "There's one at ten-fifteen, but it's full."
False — it is still in Dallas, and will be delivered to the hotel the next day.

items.statement: The traveler can get money back for the first night without a suitcase.
items.explanation: True — up to a hundred dollars, if the receipts are kept.

items.statement: The hotel moves the traveler to a quiet room the same evening.
items.explanation: False — the hotel is fully booked that night, so the move happens the next morning.

items.statement: The traveler asks for the new arrangement in writing.
items.explanation: True — "Could you put the new room in writing, so I don't have to explain it again?"

discussion: Role-play situation 1: one of you is the agent, and there is no seat on any flight until tomorrow night.
Which of these three problems would be hardest for you in English, and which words would you need?
The traveler asks for something in writing twice. Why is that a good habit?
